advances: For every integer and continuous dimension, equal positive original integer-fiber volumes give a midpoint-closed graph of actual volume centroids. A self-contained finite-set Helly argument bounds the graph's Helly number by \(2^n\). Selecting an atomic centerpoint on this actual graph and transferring its depth through the actual fiber-centroid caps proves the locked inequality on this entire equal-volume class with \(c_0=1/(2e)\). The continuous centroid-rank factor is absent for this class. This is a class theorem, not a final claim for arbitrary original fiber volumes.
author: research-agent
external_sources:
Richard J. Gardner, “The Brunn-Minkowski Inequality,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 39 (2002), 355–405, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-02-00941-2). The [author's primary manuscript dated October 25, 2001](https://faculty.gardner.wwu.edu/gorizia12.pdf), introduction equation (1) and Section 6, manuscript pages 1 and 10, states the form used: for convex bodies \(K,L\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), \(\operatorname{vol}_d((1-\lambda)K+\lambda L)^{1/d}\ge(1-\lambda)\operatorname{vol}_d(K)^{1/d}+\lambda\operatorname{vol}_d(L)^{1/d}\), with equality if and only if the bodies are positive homothets. In (3), both bodies are actual compact positive-volume fibers, \(\lambda=1/2\), and their Minkowski average is compact and hence measurable. Equal positive volumes force the homothety factor to be one. The interval case \(d=1\) is also checked directly above.

The centroid-cap input is consumed from accepted fact \(\texttt{6769574fc1bd9f8d}\) at full actual fiber mass. The finite-support centerpoint construction is consumed from accepted fact \(\texttt{c6b7777f667984de}\), with the stated location-set substitution, and its finite-set argument is included above. The required graph Helly bound is proved in this packet without importing a pending result or an external Helly characterization.
proof:
Compactness of \(C\) implies that only finitely many integer bases have nonempty fibers. Thus all the sums above are finite. Zero-volume fibers contribute zero to every halfspace-volume sum, and hence \(W=\mathcal H_d(S)\). If \(W=0\), choose any point of the assumed nonempty \(S\); all depths are nonnegative, proving the asserted zero-volume case. For the rest of the proof, \(W>0\), so \(D_+\) is finite and nonempty. Put \(N=|D_+|\). The common-volume assumption gives \(W=Nw\) and \(p_z=1/N\).

Each \(C_z\), \(z\in D_+\), is a compact convex set with positive \(d\)-volume, so it is a convex body in \(\mathbb R^d\). In accepted fact \(\texttt{6769574fc1bd9f8d}\), the density \(f\equiv1\) at mass \(m=w\) represents its true centroid \(b_z\). Therefore \(b_z\in\mathsf M_w(C_z)\subseteq C_z\), and that fact also yields

\[
\operatorname{vol}_d\bigl(C_z\cap\{y:\beta\cdot(y-b_z)\ge0\}\bigr)
\ge\gamma_d w
\qquad(\beta\in\mathbb R^d).
\tag{2}
\]

For \(\beta\ne0\), this is the containing closed-halfspace conclusion of that fact. For \(\beta=0\), the set on the left is all of \(C_z\), and (2) follows from \(\gamma_d\le1\). In particular, \(G\subseteq S\), with precisely one point for each base in \(D_+\).

We first prove the exact same-parity midpoint closure of \(G\). Let \(x,y\in D_+\) have \(x\equiv y\pmod2\) coordinatewise, and put \(u=(x+y)/2\in\mathbb Z^n\). Convexity of the one original body gives \((C_x+C_y)/2\subseteq C_u\). By the Brunn-Minkowski inequality for positive-volume convex bodies,

\[
\operatorname{vol}_d(C_u)^{1/d}
\ge\operatorname{vol}_d\bigl((C_x+C_y)/2\bigr)^{1/d}
\ge\frac{w^{1/d}+w^{1/d}}2=w^{1/d}>0.
\tag{3}
\]

Thus \(u\in D_+\) before the common-volume hypothesis is applied at \(u\). That hypothesis now gives \(\operatorname{vol}_d(C_u)=w\), so both inequalities in (3) are equalities. Equality in Brunn-Minkowski for convex bodies makes \(C_x\) and \(C_y\) positive homothets. Their equal positive volumes make the dilation factor one: \(C_y=C_x+t\) for some \(t\in\mathbb R^d\). This also includes \(d=1\), where the two equal-length intervals are translates. Consequently \((C_x+C_y)/2=C_x+t/2\), and \(b_y=b_x+t\). The inclusion of this Minkowski average in \(C_u\), together with their equal volumes, gives \(\operatorname{vol}_d(C_u\setminus(C_x+t/2))=0\). Their centroid integrals therefore agree, proving

\[
b_u=b_x+t/2=(b_x+b_y)/2,
\qquad
\frac{(x,b_x)+(y,b_y)}2=(u,b_u)\in G.
\tag{4}
\]

For \(x=y\), (4) is immediate. Thus every same-base-parity pair of graph points has its exact Euclidean midpoint in the actual graph.

We next give the finite-set Helly proof needed here. We prove the following claim directly: if a nonempty finite set \(T\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d\) contains the midpoint of every pair whose first \(n\) coordinates have the same parity, then every finite family of convex ambient sets whose common intersection misses \(T\) has a subfamily of at most \(2^n\) whose common intersection also misses \(T\).

First consider a finite family of proper closed halfspaces with common intersection disjoint from \(T\). Choose an inclusionwise minimal such subfamily and write it as \(H_i=\{v:\ell_i(v)\le\tau_i\}\), \(1\le i\le m\), where each \(\ell_i\) is a nonzero linear functional and each \(\tau_i\) is real. Minimality supplies a point \(x_i\in T\) satisfying \(\ell_j(x_i)\le\tau_j\) for every \(j\ne i\), and necessarily \(\ell_i(x_i)>\tau_i\). This statement includes \(m=1\), because \(T\) is nonempty.

Since \(T\) is finite and no point satisfies all the inequalities, the number \(\delta=\min_{s\in T}\max_{1\le i\le m}(\ell_i(s)-\tau_i)\) is positive. Choose \(0<\varepsilon<\delta\). Let \(B\) be the set of offset vectors \(v\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying

\[
v_i\ge\tau_i+\varepsilon\quad(1\le i\le m),
\qquad
\text{for every }s\in T\text{ there is an }i\text{ with }\ell_i(s)\ge v_i.
\tag{5}
\]

The vector \((\tau_i+\varepsilon)_{i=1}^m\) belongs to \(B\), so \(B\ne\varnothing\). The second condition in (5) says precisely that the open polyhedron \(\{s:\ell_i(s)<v_i\text{ for all }i\}\) misses \(T\). It is a finite intersection, over \(s\in T\), of finite unions of closed coordinate halfspaces in offset space, so \(B\) is closed. Moreover, for every \(v\in B\), the witness \(x_i\) has \(\ell_j(x_i)\le\tau_j<v_j\) for all \(j\ne i\); (5) therefore forces \(v_i\le\ell_i(x_i)\). These upper bounds and the lower bounds in (5) make \(B\) compact. Choose \(\sigma\in B\) maximizing \(\sum_{i=1}^m v_i\).

For each \(i\), there is a point \(s_i\in T\) such that

\[
\ell_i(s_i)=\sigma_i,
\qquad
\ell_j(s_i)<\sigma_j\quad(j\ne i).
\tag{6}
\]

Indeed, the finite set \(E_i=\{s\in T:\ell_j(s)<\sigma_j\text{ for all }j\ne i\}\) contains \(x_i\). Every member of \(E_i\) has \(\ell_i(s)\ge\sigma_i\) by (5). If each inequality were strict, their finitely many positive gaps would have a positive minimum. Increasing \(\sigma_i\) by less than that minimum would still satisfy (5), since only members of \(E_i\) could become interior points. This would increase the maximized sum, a contradiction. Equality for some member proves (6).

The points \(s_i\) are distinct: if \(i\ne j\), (6) makes \(\ell_i(s_i)=\sigma_i\) but \(\ell_i(s_j)<\sigma_i\). If \(m>2^n\), two of their integer bases have the same coordinatewise parity. Let these points be \(s_i,s_j\). Their midpoint belongs to \(T\) by hypothesis, whereas (6) gives \(\ell_k((s_i+s_j)/2)<\sigma_k\) for every \(k\): for \(k=i\) or \(k=j\), one endpoint inequality is an equality and the other is strict; for every other \(k\), both are strict. This contradicts (5). Thus \(m\le2^n\), proving the claim for halfspaces.

Now let \(\mathcal F\) be a finite family of arbitrary convex ambient sets whose common intersection misses \(T\). If one member has empty trace on \(T\), it is the required one-set subfamily. Otherwise, for each \(F\in\mathcal F\) and each \(s\in T\setminus F\), strictly separate the point \(s\) from the nonempty compact convex set \(\operatorname{conv}(T\cap F)\). This is possible because that convex hull is contained in \(F\), so it does not contain \(s\). The resulting closed halfspace contains \(T\cap F\) and excludes \(s\). For each \(F\), the intersection of its finitely many separating halfspaces has trace on \(T\) exactly \(T\cap F\). The union of these finite halfspace families consequently has common intersection disjoint from \(T\). By the halfspace result, at most \(2^n\) of them already have that property. Take the corresponding members of \(\mathcal F\), omitting repetitions. A point of \(T\) in all these members would belong to every chosen halfspace, which is impossible. This proves the claim for convex sets. In particular, (4) applies it to \(T=G\), and the Helly number of convex-set traces on \(G\) is at most \(h=2^n\).

Apply the finite-support atomic centerpoint construction in the proof of accepted fact \(\texttt{c6b7777f667984de}\) with ambient affine space \(\mathbb R^{n+d}\), closed location set \(T=G\), probability \(\nu=\sum_{z\in D_+}p_z\delta_{(z,b_z)}\), and Helly bound \(h=2^n\). Its location-set hypothesis is exactly the Helly claim just proved. For completeness, its finite-set argument here is as follows. Consider all closed halfspaces \(J\) with \(\nu(J)>1-1/h\). Any at most \(h\) of them have a common support point, because their complements have total mass strictly less than one. Helly therefore gives a common point of \(G\) for every finite subfamily. Since \(G\) itself is finite, this gives one common point \(q\in G\) for the entire family: otherwise, choosing one excluding halfspace for each point of \(G\) would give a finite subfamily with no common point in \(G\).

Every closed halfspace \(J\) containing this \(q\) has \(\nu(J)\ge1/h\). To check the boundary issue, suppose \(J=\{v:\ell(v)\ge t\}\) contains \(q\) but has mass less than \(1/h\). Its open complement has mass greater than \(1-1/h\). Finite support supplies \(\eta>0\) such that every support point in that complement satisfies \(\ell(v)\le t-\eta\). Thus the closed halfspace \(\{v:\ell(v)\le t-\eta\}\) has mass greater than \(1-1/h\), so it belongs to the defining family, but excludes \(q\), a contradiction. The full-space case has mass one. We have therefore selected one actual graph point \(\mathbf y^\star=q=(z^\star,b_{z^\star})\in S\), before any subsequently tested halfspace, with atomic depth at least \(2^{-n}\).

Finally let \(H\) be any proper closed ambient halfspace containing \(\mathbf y^\star\). Write \(H=\{(z,y):\alpha\cdot z+\beta\cdot y\ge t\}\), with \((\alpha,\beta)\ne0\). The graph points satisfying \(\alpha\cdot z+\beta\cdot b_z\ge t\) have original total probability at least \(2^{-n}\). For every such base, the actual-fiber event \(\beta\cdot(y-b_z)\ge0\) implies \((z,y)\in H\). Using (2) gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)
&=\sum_{z\in D_+}\operatorname{vol}_d\{y\in C_z:(z,y)\in H\}\\
&\ge\gamma_d\sum_{\substack{z\in D_+\\\alpha\cdot z+\beta\cdot b_z\ge t}}w_z
=\gamma_d W\sum_{\substack{z\in D_+\\\alpha\cdot z+\beta\cdot b_z\ge t}}p_z
\ge\gamma_d 2^{-n}W.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]

This uses the original uniform law on each actual \(C_z\), with \(p_z=w_z/W=1/N\); no synthetic fiber distribution or replaced centroid enters (7). When \(\beta=0\), the selected fibers lie entirely in \(H\), and the same bound remains valid. If the whole space is allowed as an improper halfspace, its volume is \(W\), which also satisfies (7). Taking the infimum over all containing halfspaces proves (1).

For \(d\ge1\), \(\log(1+1/d)<1/d\) gives \(\log\gamma_d=-d\log(1+1/d)>-1\), hence \(\gamma_d>1/e\). Therefore (1) implies the stated class bound with the fixed absolute \(c_0=1/(2e)\), uniformly over all \(n,d\). Zero-volume fibers were retained in \(S\) and contribute zero throughout; they impose no additional hypothesis.
statement:
Let \(n,d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body, and suppose \(S=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\ne\varnothing\). For \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), define

\[
C_z=\{y\in\mathbb R^d:(z,y)\in C\},\qquad
w_z=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z),\qquad
D_+=\{z:w_z>0\},\qquad
W=\sum_{z\in D_+}w_z=\mathcal H_d(S).
\]

Here the volume of an empty fiber is zero, and the mixed-integer halfspace depth is

\[
h_S(q)=\inf_{\substack{H\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+d}\text{ a closed halfspace}\\q\in H}}
\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\operatorname{vol}_d\{y\in C_z:(z,y)\in H\}.
\]

Assume that if \(D_+\ne\varnothing\), then there is one \(w>0\) such that \(w_z=w\) for every \(z\in D_+\). When \(W>0\), define the true original volume centroids and their original probabilities by

\[
b_z=\frac1{w_z}\int_{C_z}y\,dy,\qquad
p_z=\frac{w_z}{W}\quad(z\in D_+),\qquad
G=\{(z,b_z):z\in D_+\},\qquad
\gamma_d=\left(\frac d{d+1}\right)^d.
\]

If \(W>0\), there is one \(z^\star\in D_+\) such that the fixed actual point \(\mathbf y^\star=(z^\star,b_{z^\star})\in G\subseteq S\) satisfies

\[
h_S(\mathbf y^\star)\ge\frac{\gamma_d}{2^n}W.
\tag{1}
\]

Consequently, on this class, for the absolute constant \(c_0=1/(2e)\in(0,1/e)\), there is one \(\mathbf y^\star\in S\) such that every closed halfspace \(H\) containing it satisfies \(\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\ge c_0 2^{-n}\mathcal H_d(S)\). If \(W=0\), this last assertion holds for every point of \(S\).

The symbols \(C_z,w_z,D_+,W,b_z,p_z,\gamma_d\) have exactly the meanings in accepted fact \(\texttt{c6b7777f667984de}\). The metronoid \(\mathsf M_m\) below has exactly the meaning in accepted fact \(\texttt{6769574fc1bd9f8d}\); it is used on \(C_z\) with its full mass \(m=w_z=w\). No affine dependence of \(b_z\) on \(z\) is assumed.
